summary: Dmitry Petrov introduces the fundamental challenge agents face with physical, unstructured data—video, sensor data, and robot telemetry—contrasting this with structured warehouses where frontier labs operate. Anthropic reported only 21% agent accuracy on data projects without specialized harnesses, and OpenAI required six layers of context engineering, but both benefit from tables, schemas, and execution engines. Physical data lacks this luxury. The core problem is scale explosion: thousands of complex binary files generate millions of nested objects—clips, frames, detected objects with classes, confidence scores, and bounding boxes—compared to a neutron star: small surface footprint, enormous mass. Conventional solutions fail: JSON metadata files on S3 create latency and inconsistency; centralized databases introduce dual-language stacks researchers find too complex. DataChain addresses this with Pydantic schemas that unify data definitions and code in Python, transpiling to SQL under the hood. A live demonstration analyzes dashcam video using Claude Code with the DataChain harness—YOLO smallest model, per-frame granularity, 91 January clips, 24-minute processing, ~100,000 records, 82 of 91 clips with people. Follow-up queries return instantly from the local materialized database. DataChain provides its own execution engine for unstructured data, supporting distributed execution with simple resource specification. Because processing binary files with LLMs is expensive, incremental updates and data checkpoints are must-haves—on failure, you fix bugs and resume without recomputing everything. Running tests in data projects is extremely slow, and accuracy is even more critical than in software because data problems typically have only one correct answer. Instead of running expensive scripts on raw data, agents organize meta-information layers using established dimensional modeling techniques (star schema, one big table). Before answering, the agent self-assesses whether it has proper datasets to respond in a single SQL-ish query; if not, it builds a reusable layer general enough for related questions. A knowledge base of MD files—containing dataset descriptions, session context, storage dependencies, data previews, statistics, and source code (the most crucial part per OpenAI's blog post)—enables sharing and prevents redundant recompute. The complete stack runs from raw unstructured data in object storage, through the compute engine extracting metadata, into materialized datasets and slices, surfaced via the knowledge base. Standard coding agents like Copilot, Codex, and Claude Code operate inefficiently in this world without a data harness because the laws of physics change.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Conventional approaches—JSON metadata on S3 or centralized databases—create latency, inconsistency, and dual-stack complexity that researchers avoid.

The full stack: raw unstructured data in object storage → compute engine → materialized datasets → knowledge base → data lineage connecting everything.

sections.title: Introduction: Physical Data Challenges
sections.summary: Dmitry introduces agents failing at physical data work and cites Anthropic's 21% accuracy and OpenAI's six context layers, noting both operate in structured warehouses—a luxury absent in the unstructured data world.

sections.title: The Neutron Star Problem and Failed Solutions
sections.summary: Explains how thousands of complex binary files explode into millions of nested objects (neutron star metaphor) and why JSON-on-S3 (latency, inconsistency) and centralized databases (dual-stack complexity) both fail for researchers.

sections.title: DataChain Schema Approach with Pydantic
sections.summary: Introduces Pydantic schemas as the unifying solution: same language for data, schemas, and code; no SQL islands; transpiles to SQL under the hood. Emphasizes this problem is specific to physical data, not structured data.

sections.title: Live Demo: Dashcam Video Analysis
sections.summary: Demonstrates DataChain with Claude Code on dashcam data—YOLO smallest model, per-frame granularity, 91 January clips, 24-minute processing, 82/91 clips with people, ~100,000 records, instant query from local database.

sections.title: Generated Data Model and Source Code Review
sections.summary: Reviews the agent-generated Pydantic data model: file metadata (path, checksum, e-tag, size), frame ID, timestamp, class ID, confidence score, bounding box—stored as database rows instead of S3 JSONs, enabling fast analytical queries.

sections.title: Execution Engine for Unstructured Data
sections.summary: Discusses DataChain's execution engine connecting Python functions, Pydantic schemas, storage, and warehouse holistically; supports distributed execution (e.g., 40 machines) with mapper/generator patterns; emphasizes cost of losing intermediate results when processing with LLMs.

sections.title: Incremental Updates and Data Checkpoints
sections.summary: Explains that incremental updates and data checkpoints are must-haves: on failure, fix bugs and resume without recomputing everything; new files in the bucket trigger only new processing. Notes that testing in data projects is super slow and accuracy is more critical since data problems typically have only one correct answer.

sections.title: Meta-Information Layers and Agent Self-Assessment
sections.summary: Advocates stopping expensive Python-on-raw-data execution and instead organizing meta-information layers using established dimensional modeling (star schema, one big table). Agents self-assess whether proper datasets exist for fast SQL-ish queries; if not, they build reusable layers general enough for related questions.

sections.title: Knowledge Base and Data Lineage
sections.summary: Describes knowledge base as MD files containing dataset description, session context, storage dependencies, data preview, statistics, and source code (most crucial per OpenAI's blog post). Source data, source code, and warehouse results form connected data lineage shared across teammates to prevent redundant recompute.

sections.title: The Full Stack and Conclusion
sections.summary: Presents the complete stack: raw unstructured data in object storage at the bottom, compute engine extracting metadata, materialized datasets and slices, and knowledge base for sharing. Standard coding agents fail here because laws of physics change; the solution is a data harness, not stronger models. DataChain implements these principles as open source.
